incident_text: Customers see 'order pending' for minutes after placing an order, and some retry. Started around 10:00.

E-001.claim: order-router error rate peaked at 0.08 in the window, against a minimum of 0.003, which suggests errors on the order path.
E-001.author: observability

E-002.claim: order-router latency reached 548.978 ms at peak, from a minimum of 170.47 ms, and was still 510.288 ms at the last sample.
E-002.author: observability

E-003.claim: broker-gateway had the highest error rate in the window, peaking at 0.106 with 0.106 still at the last sample.
E-003.author: observability

E-004.claim: broker-gateway latency peaked at 695.886 ms, from a minimum of 202.757 ms.
E-004.author: observability

E-005.claim: broker-gateway rate_limit_remaining stayed high (minimum 855.106), which weakens a rate-limit exhaustion explanation for the broker errors.
E-005.author: observability

E-006.claim: orchestrator error rate reached 0.033 and latency reached 1108.833 ms, both elevated relative to their minimums, though its rise is smaller than the downstream order-path rises.
E-006.author: observability

E-007.claim: wa-webhook looks healthy in the window: error rate stayed at or below 0.003 and latency at or below 86.131 ms.
E-007.author: observability

E-008.claim: msg-delivery looks healthy: error rate peaked at 0.005, latency at 275.736 ms, and restarts_5m was 0.0 throughout.
E-008.author: observability

E-009.claim: order-router throughput averaged 19.859 rps, compared with 54.939 rps for orchestrator and 40.134 rps for broker-gateway, so order-router carries much less traffic than the orchestrator in this window.
E-009.author: observability

E-010.claim: The order path degrades at broker-gateway and order-router, and orchestrator is affected second. The retries that customers see are probably a response to slow confirmations, but this is not yet confirmed.
E-010.author: observability

E-011.claim: rabbitmq aggregate rps over the window ranged from 184.71 to 211.296 (mean 199.545); this is not per-queue and is not split into publish vs consume.
E-011.author: observability

E-012.claim: rabbitmq err_rate was 0.0 for the whole window, and latency_ms stayed between 1.867 and 2.137.
E-012.author: observability

E-013.claim: rabbitmq returned no WARN-or-higher log lines in 09:30-11:00. The result was not truncated or partial.
E-013.author: observability

E-014.claim: redis-cache evicted_keys was 0.0 across the window, so no eviction pressure is visible.
E-014.author: observability

E-015.claim: redis-cache hit_ratio mean was 0.958, but its max of 1.022 is above 1.0, which is not a valid ratio and suggests a metric artifact.
E-015.author: observability

E-017.claim: postgres pool_waiting was 0.0 for the whole window, so there is no connection-pool queuing.
E-017.author: observability

E-018.claim: postgres latency_ms peaked at 8.551 (mean 8.011), and replication_lag_s stayed at or below 0.417.
E-018.author: observability

E-019.claim: postgres slow_queries stayed near 1, between 0.934 and 1.046, with no spike.
E-019.author: observability

E-020.claim: portfolio-consumer rps ran at about 37-43 (mean 39.984), and latency_ms peaked at 160.946. Both are summary-level values without a time series.
E-020.author: observability

E-021.claim: portfolio-consumer err_rate peaked at 0.004 (mean 0.003), so its error rate is low.
E-021.author: observability

E-022.claim: The rabbitmq rps metric is aggregate across all queues. Because it does not split by queue, it cannot show whether portfolio-updates is consuming more slowly than it is published to.
E-022.author: observability

E-023.claim: order-router deployed at 09:50 UTC with a log-level change, about 10 minutes before the reported 10:00 onset. This is a candidate only; the note suggests low risk.
E-023.author: dependency

E-024.claim: orchestrator deployed orchestrator-00669 at 09:18 UTC, described as a minor copy change.
E-024.author: dependency

E-025.claim: orchestrator deployed orchestrator-00952 at 09:24 UTC, described as a metrics label rename. This is unlikely to affect order flow.
E-025.author: dependency

E-026.claim: wa-webhook deployed wa-webhook-00939 at 09:25 UTC, described as a minor copy change. wa-webhook is the inbound entry point, so this is a weak candidate.
E-026.author: dependency

E-027.claim: The change query covered deploys, config, migrations and flags for all services in the window and returned only these four items. No config, migration or flag change was recorded between 08:00 and 10:15.
E-027.author: dependency

E-028.claim: Dependency lookup for rabbitmq returned no edges, so the producers and consumers of outbound-msgs, inbound-msgs and portfolio-updates are not mapped. The order-router lookup also cannot be tied to its result with certainty (see gaps).
E-028.author: dependency

E-029.claim: Historical incident INC-0431 (2026-02-02) involved an order-router release causing order placement errors. This is a hypothesis to test against current evidence, not a confirmed match.
E-029.author: dependency

E-030.claim: order-router calls broker-gateway synchronously with the highest call weight on the order path (0.8) and calls postgres (0.3). web-app calls order-router (weight 0.5).
E-030.author: dependency

E-031.claim: order-router has a synchronous dependency on postgres.
E-031.author: dependency

E-032.claim: orchestrator calls llm-gateway (0.7), portfolio-svc (0.4), broker-gateway (0.3), market-data (0.2), auth-kyc (0.1) and redis-cache (0.3) synchronously. broker-gateway and redis-cache are shared with other order-path services.
E-032.author: dependency

E-033.claim: orchestrator publishes to outbound-msgs and consumes from inbound-msgs. These are the only queue links returned for orchestrator.
E-033.author: dependency

E-034.claim: order-router has no queue links and no callers other than web-app. Its only dependencies are broker-gateway and postgres.
E-034.author: dependency

E-035.claim: Deploy orchestrator-00669 (minor copy change) at 09:18 UTC, about 42 minutes before onset. It is a candidate only, since orchestrator is upstream of the order path.
E-035.author: dependency

E-036.claim: Deploy orchestrator-00952 (metrics label rename) at 09:24 UTC. A metrics-only change is unlikely to affect order flow.
E-036.author: dependency

E-037.claim: Deploy wa-webhook-00939 (minor copy change) at 09:25 UTC, upstream of the order path.
E-037.author: dependency

E-038.claim: Deploy order-router-00455 (log level tweak) at 09:50 UTC, 10 minutes before onset. order-router sits on the order path to broker-gateway and postgres, so it is the closest candidate, though a log-level change is unlikely to be causal.
E-038.author: dependency

E-039.claim: The change query covered deploy, config, migration and flag kinds for 09:00 to 11:00 UTC, and it returned only the four deploys above. No config, migration or flag change was found near onset.
E-039.author: dependency

E-040.claim: rabbitmq returned no dependency edges, so the producer and consumer links for inbound-msgs, outbound-msgs and portfolio-updates are not confirmed.
E-040.author: dependency

E-041.claim: The 'pending' status is probably set by orchestrator when it accepts an order and cleared by a callback or consumer, and portfolio-consumer or msg-delivery may carry the confirmation. This is inferred from service names and is not confirmed by any tool result.
E-041.author: dependency

E-042.claim: Shared-resource contention is plausible at broker-gateway (called by both orchestrator and order-router) and at redis-cache and postgres, but no data here shows saturation.
E-042.author: dependency

E-043.claim: Past incident INC-0431 (2026-02-02) was attributed to a validation regression in an order-router release and fixed by rolling back the order-router revision. This is a hint only: its symptom was order placement errors, not orders stuck pending.
E-043.author: dependency

E-044.claim: Past incident INC-0431 fix was a rollback of the order-router revision.
E-044.author: dependency

E-045.claim: Past incident INC-0412 (2026-01-18) was caused by a redis restart evicting hot context, which led to a cache stampede on portfolio-svc. This is a hint only: its symptom was late balance notifications.
E-045.excerpt: Redis restart evicted hot context, cache stampede on portfolio-svc
E-045.author: dependency

E-046.claim: Neither past incident closely resembles the current case (orders stuck pending, customer retries, delays starting around 10:00 UTC on 2026-03-31). The current cause could differ from both.
E-046.author: dependency

E-047.claim: A redis restart or order-router release around 10:00 UTC on 2026-03-31 would be a candidate worth checking, since the past incidents point to those components. This has not been verified.
E-047.author: dependency

E-048.claim: broker-gateway latency_ms steps up at 10:00, from about 220 ms at 09:59 to 331 ms, and reaches 695.886 at 10:04 (no departure before 10:00 in the 09:50-09:59 samples).
E-048.author: observability

E-049.claim: broker-gateway err_rate steps up at 10:00 from 0.004 to 0.03 and reaches 0.106 by 10:04.
E-049.author: observability

E-050.claim: order-router latency_ms steps up at 10:00 from 179.594 to 250.733 and reaches 548.978 at 10:04.
E-050.author: observability

E-051.claim: order-router err_rate steps up at 10:00 from 0.005 to 0.019 and reaches 0.079 by 10:03.
E-051.author: observability

E-052.claim: The order-router deploy at 09:50 shows no latency step: the 09:50 sample is within the 09:30-09:59 range, which runs about 170-190 ms.
E-052.author: observability

E-053.claim: orchestrator latency_ms is already elevated before 10:00 (values of 862-956 ms through 09:30-09:59) and rises more clearly after about 10:03, so it has no clean step at 10:00.
E-053.author: observability

E-054.claim: Broker-gateway and order-router degrade at effectively the same minute. Sub-minute ordering and the 2:1 rps ratio (not yet pulled) cannot settle whether broker-gateway caused order-router's rise or the reverse. A retry loop amplifying load is still plausible but untested.
E-054.author: observability

E-055.claim: The 10:00 onset matches the customer report, but the 09:50 order-router deploy shows no metric change at the time it happened, which weakens it as the trigger; this is inferred from the absence of a step, not from a rollback test.
E-055.author: observability

E-056.claim: broker-gateway's earliest WARN is a single slow broker response at 09:46:07Z, about 14 minutes before onset. 10 'broker responded slowly once' lines appear in the window (my tally).
E-056.excerpt: 2026-03-31T09:46:07Z WARN broker-gateway: broker responded slowly once for request 261701
E-056.author: observability

E-057.claim: Sustained slow GET /orders/status responses at broker-gateway begin at 10:00:03Z, matching the reported onset.
E-057.excerpt: 2026-03-31T10:00:03Z WARN broker-gateway: order status endpoint slow: GET /orders/status took 331ms
E-057.author: observability

E-058.claim: The slow GET /orders/status duration grows over the window. 120 such lines appear (my tally: 130 total minus 10 'slow once' lines).
E-058.excerpt: 2026-03-31T10:04:01Z WARN broker-gateway: order status endpoint slow: GET /orders/status took 696ms
E-058.author: observability

E-059.claim: broker-gateway returned 130 WARN-or-higher lines in 09:45-10:30. None are ERROR, and no 5xx or connection error is logged by broker-gateway. The result was not truncated or partial.
E-059.author: observability

E-060.claim: order-router's first broker-related failure is an ERROR at 10:00:32Z, about 32 seconds after the first broker-gateway slow status call. Across the window, 30 'broker-gateway call failed: HTTP 503' ERRORs appear (my tally).
E-060.excerpt: 2026-03-31T10:00:32Z ERROR order-router: broker-gateway call failed: HTTP 503
E-060.author: observability

E-061.claim: order-router's first upstream timeout to broker-gateway is at 10:01:14Z. 59 such timeouts appear in the window (my tally).
E-061.excerpt: 2026-03-31T10:01:14Z WARN order-router: upstream call to broker-gateway timed out after 438ms
E-061.author: observability

E-062.claim: order-router logged no ERROR and no broker timeout before 10:00:32Z. Its only earlier WARN lines are 'validation warning: price near circuit limit' entries, which are present at 09:45-09:59 and also recur through the incident, so they do not mark the onset.
E-062.excerpt: 2026-03-31T09:45:28Z WARN order-router: order 79231 validation warning: price near circuit limit
E-062.author: observability

E-063.claim: order-router's err_rate summary: min 0.003, max 0.08, last 0.079.
E-063.excerpt: order-router err_rate stats min 0.003, max 0.08, mean 0.051, last 0.079, missing 0
E-063.author: observability

E-064.claim: order-router latency_ms summary: min 170.754, max 548.978, last 482.51. This differs from the established E-002 values (min 170.47, last 510.288).
E-064.excerpt: order-router latency_ms stats min 170.754, max 548.978, mean 394.111, last 482.51, missing 0
E-064.author: observability

E-065.claim: order-router rps shows no visible volume change in the window. The summary is flat, and the mean is 19.955 rather than the 19.859 in E-009.
E-065.excerpt: order-router rps stats min 18.592, max 21.312, mean 19.955, last 19.989, missing 0
E-065.author: observability

E-066.claim: order-router's timeout durations match broker-gateway's slow status durations (for example 438ms at 10:01:01-10:01:53Z on the broker side and 'timed out after 438ms' at 10:01:14Z). This suggests order-router is timing out against a broker that is already slow, so broker latency is the likely first cause and order-router's errors are downstream. This is not proven: the logs do not show broker-side timing for the same request IDs.
E-066.author: observability

E-067.claim: No retry or duplicate-submission messages appear in either service's WARN-or-higher logs. This is an absence within the queried level, and INFO or DEBUG logs were not searched, so it does not rule out retries.
E-067.author: observability

E-068.claim: outbound-msgs queue depth was zero across the window, with no DLQ backlog, and 4 consumers.
E-068.author: observability

E-069.claim: outbound-msgs consume_rate averaged above publish_rate (consume mean 63.848 vs publish mean 54.785), so no backlog build-up is visible on average.
E-069.author: observability

E-070.claim: inbound-msgs queue depth rose to 30.133 at the last sample, with a window mean of 6.487.
E-070.author: observability

E-071.claim: inbound-msgs redeliveries were elevated, with a max of 4.161 and last value of 3.742, against a min of 0.403.
E-071.author: observability

E-072.claim: At the last sample, inbound-msgs consume_rate (58.244) was below publish_rate (59.744), which is consistent with consumers falling slightly behind. The window averages still show consume above publish (64.37 vs 59.92).
E-072.author: observability

E-073.claim: portfolio-updates depth was zero across the window, with no DLQ, and 3 consumers. Consume rate averaged above publish rate (49.239 vs 40.213), which weakens a portfolio-updates backlog explanation.
E-073.author: observability

E-074.claim: msg-delivery rps and latency were steady in the window: latency_ms mean 250.141 and max 272.245, rps mean 54.846, restarts_5m 0.0.
E-074.author: observability

E-075.claim: msg-delivery err_rate peaked at 0.005, which is consistent with the earlier healthy assessment.
E-075.author: observability

E-076.claim: portfolio-consumer rps averaged 40.114 and latency_ms peaked at 160.946, with err_rate max 0.004.
E-076.author: observability

E-077.claim: The inbound-msgs depth and redelivery rise may be a secondary contributor to 'pending' if consumers lag, but the onset relative to 10:00 UTC is unknown without a time series. It is not a confirmed cause.
E-077.author: observability

E-078.claim: broker-gateway latency_ms was at baseline at 09:59 and jumped at 10:00, the first minute of deviation.
E-078.author: observability

E-079.claim: order-router latency_ms was at baseline at 09:59 and jumped at 10:00, in the same minute as broker-gateway.
E-079.author: observability

E-080.claim: broker-gateway err_rate rose from baseline at 09:59 to 0.03 at 10:00, and kept climbing to 0.054 at 10:01.
E-080.author: observability

E-081.claim: order-router err_rate rose from baseline at 09:59 to 0.019 at 10:00, in the same minute as broker-gateway, and to 0.037 at 10:01.
E-081.author: observability

E-082.claim: Broker-gateway's larger first-minute deviation is consistent with it being the origin of the slowdown, since order-router calls it synchronously (E-030). But the 1-minute step cannot separate a few seconds of lead, so this ordering is not confirmed.
E-082.author: observability

E-083.claim: Because both services degrade at the same minute, a shared upstream factor (for example a broker-side dependency or shared resource) could also explain the pattern. The metrics here do not identify one.
E-083.author: observability

E-084.claim: The first broker-gateway WARN in the window was a single slow broker response, at 09:46:07, which is well before the 10:00 onset.
E-084.excerpt: 2026-03-31T09:46:07Z WARN broker-gateway: broker responded slowly once for request 261701
E-084.author: observability

E-085.claim: The order status endpoint slow-warning series starts at 10:00:03, which matches the reported onset. The first recorded duration is 331ms.
E-085.excerpt: 2026-03-31T10:00:03Z WARN broker-gateway: order status endpoint slow: GET /orders/status took 331ms
E-085.author: observability

E-086.claim: Order status durations climbed over the first few minutes after onset to a peak of 696ms at about 10:04.
E-086.excerpt: 2026-03-31T10:04:01Z WARN broker-gateway: order status endpoint slow: GET /orders/status took 696ms
E-086.author: observability

E-087.claim: The order status endpoint was still slow at the end of the window, at 622ms at 10:29:57. Durations stayed in the 620-690ms range from about 10:05 onward, so the slowdown did not recover.
E-087.excerpt: 2026-03-31T10:29:57Z WARN broker-gateway: order status endpoint slow: GET /orders/status took 622ms
E-087.author: observability

E-088.claim: No ERROR-level lines, 5xx responses, timeouts or connection errors appear in broker-gateway WARN+ logs for 09:45-10:30. The result was complete (not truncated or partial), so the absence is informative for WARN+ output only.
E-088.author: observability

E-089.claim: Sporadic 'broker responded slowly once' warnings occurred before onset, with 5 in 09:46-09:59. The count is 10 for the whole window, which is a low rate compared with the status-endpoint series.
E-089.excerpt: 2026-03-31T09:59:32Z WARN broker-gateway: broker responded slowly once for request 762303
E-089.author: observability

E-090.claim: The status-endpoint duration is measured at the broker-gateway boundary, so the added latency is probably in the upstream broker call. The logs do not show where the time is spent.
E-090.author: observability

E-091.claim: order-router logs its first broker-gateway call failure with HTTP 503 at 10:00:32, the 503 referenced in the task.
E-091.excerpt: 2026-03-31T10:00:32Z ERROR order-router: broker-gateway call failed: HTTP 503
E-091.author: observability

E-092.claim: orchestrator also logs HTTP 503 from broker-gateway, at 10:00:52, so the 503s are not specific to order-router.
E-092.excerpt: 2026-03-31T10:00:52Z ERROR orchestrator: broker-gateway call failed: HTTP 503
E-092.author: observability

E-093.claim: A WARN-or-higher search for '503' across all services in 09:59:50-10:01:00 returned only the two order-router and orchestrator ERROR lines. No broker-gateway line mentions 503.
E-093.author: observability

E-094.claim: broker-gateway's first sustained slow order-status response is at 10:00:03 (331ms). Before this, its only WARN lines in the window are sporadic 'slowly once' warnings.
E-094.excerpt: 2026-03-31T10:00:03Z WARN broker-gateway: order status endpoint slow: GET /orders/status took 331ms
E-094.author: observability

E-095.claim: Before the sustained slow series, broker-gateway's last sporadic warning is at 09:59:32 and is a single slow broker response.
E-095.excerpt: 2026-03-31T09:59:32Z WARN broker-gateway: broker responded slowly once for request 762303
E-095.author: observability

E-096.claim: Status-endpoint durations keep climbing after onset, reaching 696ms by 10:04:01 and still reaching 684ms at 10:09:01 (no recovery).
E-096.excerpt: 2026-03-31T10:04:01Z WARN broker-gateway: order status endpoint slow: GET /orders/status took 696ms
E-096.author: observability

E-097.claim: broker-gateway err_rate summary over the window: min 0.004, max 0.106, last 0.106. This matches the rise recorded in E-003.
E-097.author: observability

E-098.claim: broker-gateway latency_ms summary: min 202.757, max 695.886, last 684.236.
E-098.author: observability

E-099.claim: broker-gateway rate_limit_remaining stayed high (min 858.816, max 922.837) during the window, which weakens a rate-limit cause for the 503s.
E-099.author: observability

E-100.claim: The metric query asked for 1-minute points, but none were returned, so the per-minute step at 10:00 cannot be checked in this call.
E-100.author: observability

E-101.claim: The metric list for broker-gateway has four metrics (err_rate, latency_ms, rate_limit_remaining, rps) and none is a 5xx count, status-class or upstream-broker-call metric.
E-101.author: observability

E-102.claim: broker-gateway's INFO lines show 'broker order status ok' interleaved with the slow warnings during the incident (for example at 10:06:00). These lines carry no durations, so they do not show whether those calls were slow.
E-102.excerpt: 2026-03-31T10:06:00Z INFO broker-gateway: broker order status ok
E-102.author: observability

E-103.claim: The 503 is probably produced between order-router and the broker-gateway application (a proxy, load balancer, circuit breaker or relayed broker response). broker-gateway's app logs show no error for it, so the origin is not confirmed by these logs.
E-103.author: observability

E-104.claim: Order-router's 503 at 10:00:32 comes about 29 seconds after broker-gateway's first slow status call at 10:00:03 (not 32 seconds as E-060 states). This is derived from the two timestamps.
E-104.author: observability

E-105.claim: inbound-msgs redeliveries were at baseline at 09:59 and jumped to 1.323 at 10:00, the same minute as the reported onset. The pre-onset window maximum was 0.742 (09:35).
E-105.author: observability

E-106.claim: inbound-msgs redeliveries kept climbing after onset and plateaued at about 3.6-4.2 from 10:04 onward. The series stayed elevated through 10:29, with last value 3.742.
E-106.author: observability

E-107.claim: inbound-msgs consume_rate was at 65.843 at 09:59 and fell from 10:02 onward, reaching 55.015 at 10:04.
E-107.author: observability

E-108.claim: inbound-msgs consume_rate was already dropping at 10:02 (63.574), after 67.873 at 10:00 and 67.186 at 10:01. This is a dip that begins about 2 minutes after onset, not at 10:00.
E-108.author: observability

E-109.claim: inbound-msgs queue depth was 0.0 from 09:30 through 10:03 and first became non-zero at 10:04 (3.68). That is after the 10:00 onset.
E-109.author: observability

E-110.claim: inbound-msgs depth fell back to 0.0 at 10:07 between non-zero minutes, so the build-up is not monotonic. Depth then grew steadily from about 10:09 and reached 30.133 at 10:29 (last sample).
E-110.author: observability

E-111.claim: inbound-msgs depth reached 30.133 at the last sample (10:29), with window mean 6.487.
E-111.author: observability

E-112.claim: inbound-msgs publish_rate showed no step at 10:00. It was 59.569 at 09:59 and 58.079 at 10:00, within its normal range. The window range was 56.814 to 63.157.
E-112.author: observability

E-113.claim: At 10:04, inbound-msgs consume_rate (55.015) was below publish_rate (58.695). Consume is mixed afterward, with consume below publish at 10:09 (55.708 vs 60.406) and above at 10:05 and 10:07. At the last sample consume (58.244) was below publish (59.744).
E-113.author: observability

E-114.claim: order-router rps shows no rise after 10:00. The window max (21.312 at 10:11) is only modestly above the pre-onset max of 20.709 at 09:40. The window mean is 19.886 and the last value is 19.989.
E-114.author: observability

E-115.claim: order-router rps at 10:00 was 19.419, which is inside its pre-onset range, so there is no step at onset.
E-115.author: observability

E-116.claim: The redelivery rise at 10:00 is likely consumer-side nack/requeue, not new arrivals, because publish_rate stayed flat. That would point to consumers slowing (consume dip from 10:02) rather than a surge of retried messages. Not verified: no per-consumer or nack-reason data was pulled.
E-116.author: observability

E-117.claim: The inbound-msgs redelivery and depth rise is more likely a downstream effect of slow processing than an independent cause of the 10:00 onset. The 10:00 timing matches the broker-gateway and order-router latency step (E-048, E-050), but a 1-minute resolution cannot establish sub-minute order.
E-117.author: observability

E-118.claim: No deploy, config, migration or flag change was recorded for broker-gateway between 09:30 and 10:05 UTC.
E-118.author: dependency

E-119.claim: The only change across all services for deploy, config, migration and flag kinds between 09:30 and 10:05 UTC is the order-router deploy at 09:50, described as a log-level tweak. It is a candidate only and is unlikely to be causal.
E-119.author: dependency

E-120.claim: broker-gateway's callers are orchestrator (weight 0.3) and order-router (weight 0.8). The result lists no outbound synchronous callees and no queue links for broker-gateway.
E-120.author: dependency

E-121.claim: Orchestrator's calls to broker-gateway (weight 0.3) probably degraded at 10:00, since orchestrator also calls broker-gateway and its latency is elevated. This is taken from the existing claim E-053, which shows no clean 10:00 step, and my tools did not measure it, so it is not verified here.
E-121.author: dependency

E-122.claim: Because broker-gateway has no recorded internal change, the 10:00 slowdown is more likely to come from the upstream broker or a shared resource, or from a change that get_changes cannot see. This is inferred from the absence of records and is not confirmed.
E-122.author: dependency

E-123.claim: broker-gateway's first sustained slow order-status call in my pull is at 10:00:03Z, at 331ms, which matches the reported onset.
E-123.excerpt: 2026-03-31T10:00:03Z WARN broker-gateway: order status endpoint slow: GET /orders/status took 331ms
E-123.author: observability

E-124.claim: Before onset, broker-gateway logged only isolated 'responded slowly once' warnings, with no sustained status-endpoint slowness. The first is at 09:56:10Z.
E-124.excerpt: 2026-03-31T09:56:10Z WARN broker-gateway: broker responded slowly once for request 415594

H1.statement: broker-gateway's calls to the upstream broker became slow on GET /orders/status from 10:00:03 and stayed slow, so order-router (heaviest synchronous caller) timed out and got 503s, leaving orders pending and prompting customer retries.

H2.statement: A shared upstream factor outside the recorded change history (broker-side vendor issue, network path or shared infrastructure) slowed broker-gateway and its callers in the same minute, so broker-gateway is the visible symptom rather than the origin.

H3.statement: inbound-msgs consumers are falling behind (redeliveries from 10:00, consume dip from 10:02, depth from 10:04), delaying confirmations as a secondary contributor to pending orders.

T1.goal: Establish the timeline of the 'order pending' symptom around 10:00: when did order confirmation latency first rise, and which service metrics (latency, error rate, throughput, retries) for wa-webhook, orchestrator, order-router, broker-gateway, msg-delivery changed first, from about 09:30 to now?
hints: Compare against a baseline from the same time on prior days
Look for duplicate order submissions or retry spikes from customers
Identify the earliest anomalous signal, not the loudest
T1.summary: Summary metrics over 09:30-11:00 show degradation concentrated downstream of the webhook: order-router (err_rate max 0.08, latency max 548.978 ms) and broker-gateway (err_rate max 0.106, latency max 695.886 ms) both have elevated peaks, and orchestrator shows a milder rise (err_rate max 0.033, latency max 1108.833 ms). wa-webhook and msg-delivery look healthy in their summaries. These are window summaries without points or a baseline, so I could not establish when the rise began or whether it started near 10:00, and I found no evidence of retry or duplicate-submission spikes.

T2.goal: Inspect queue and datastore health from 09:30 onward: depth, age of oldest message, publish vs consume rates, and consumer counts for inbound-msgs, outbound-msgs and portfolio-updates on rabbitmq; plus redis-cache hit rate/latency/evictions and postgres connections, lock waits and slow queries. Which of these deviated, and in what order relative to the pending-order symptom?
hints: Check portfolio-consumer and msg-delivery consumer lag and unacked messages
Look for error logs, timeouts and redelivery loops in order-router, broker-gateway, llm-gateway, portfolio-svc, aa-sync, market-data, auth-kyc
Note which anomalies could be downstream effects rather than causes
T2.summary: Across rabbitmq, redis-cache, postgres and portfolio-consumer, the summary stats show no clear deviation in the 09:30-11:00 window: rabbitmq err_rate stayed at 0.0 with no WARN logs, redis evicted_keys stayed at 0.0, postgres pool_waiting stayed at 0.0, and portfolio-consumer err_rate stayed at or below 0.004. The summaries have no time series, so I could not establish onset or ordering relative to the 10:00 pending-order symptom. The tooling also did not expose the queue-level metrics this task asks for (depth, oldest-message age, per-queue publish/consume rates, consumer counts, unacked/redelivered counts), so queue health remains unverified.

T3.goal: List every change between about 08:00 and 10:15 across all listed services and infrastructure: deploys, config changes, environment or secret/credential changes, database migrations, feature flag flips, scaling or autoscaling events, rabbitmq/redis/postgres setting changes, and third-party or broker-side changes. What changed, when, and who or what made the change?
hints: Do not limit to deploys; include flags, config, migrations, certificate or token expiry, and scheduled jobs
Include cron or batch jobs such as aa-sync runs that start near 10:00
Report exact timestamps so they can be aligned with the symptom start
T3.summary: The change query for 08:00–10:15 UTC across all services, with kinds deploy, config, migration and flag, returned only four deploys and no config, migration or flag changes. The closest change to the 10:00 onset is an order-router deploy at 09:50 labelled 'log level tweak', which looks low-risk but sits on the order path. Nothing in the results shows a change at or near 10:00, and the scheduled and infrastructure-side changes the task asked about were not covered by this query.

T4.goal: Map the dependencies and queue producer/consumer links for the order path (web-app/wa-webhook -> orchestrator -> llm-gateway, auth-kyc, order-router -> broker-gateway, market-data, portfolio-svc, portfolio-consumer, msg-delivery) including which services use redis-cache, postgres and rabbitmq queues inbound-msgs, outbound-msgs, portfolio-updates. Where are synchronous vs asynchronous hops, timeouts and retry policies, and which services share resources?
hints: Identify where an order status of 'pending' is set and what event or callback moves it to confirmed
Identify shared resources that could cause cross-service contention
Distinguish upstream causes from downstream symptoms
T4.summary: The order path has a high-weight synchronous edge from order-router to broker-gateway (0.8) plus order-router to postgres (0.3), and orchestrator fans out synchronously to llm-gateway, portfolio-svc, broker-gateway, market-data, auth-kyc and redis-cache. Four deploys landed 09:18 to 09:50 UTC, about 10 to 42 minutes before the 10:00 onset, and all are described as minor (copy, metrics label, log level). No config, migration or flag changes appeared in the 09:00 to 11:00 window. The graph does not show where 'pending' is set or how the confirmation callback reaches the customer, and it gives no timeout or retry policies, so the queue and retry analysis is incomplete.

T5.goal: Find past incidents with similar symptoms (orders stuck pending, delayed confirmations, customer retries, queue backlog, broker-gateway or order-router slowness, consumer lag) and report what their causes and resolutions were and how well they resemble this one.
hints: Treat past incidents as hints only; note differences from the current case
Include incidents involving rabbitmq backlog, redis or postgres degradation, and broker or account-aggregator integrations
T5.summary: Past-incident search found no close match. Searches for rabbitmq backlog, consumer lag, broker-gateway and aa-sync slowness returned nothing relevant. The two incidents that did come back are weak hints: INC-0431 (order-router release validation regression, which produced placement errors rather than pending orders) and INC-0412 (redis restart causing a cache stampede on portfolio-svc, which produced late notifications). Neither is established as the cause here, and whether an order-router or redis change happened near 10:00 UTC needs checking against change and dependency data.

T6.goal: Pull per-minute time series from 09:30 to 10:30 for latency_ms, err_rate and rps for broker-gateway, order-router and orchestrator. Include a prior-day baseline for the same hours. State which service's latency and error rate first departed from baseline, and whether that was before or after 09:50 and 10:00.
hints: All evidence is min/max/mean over 09:30-11:00. It does not show whether broker-gateway degraded before order-router, or whether either rose before or after the 09:50 order-router deploy. Without ordering, 'broker-gateway degraded and order-router inherited it' cannot be told apart from 'order-router degraded and loaded broker-gateway' (H2). Broker-gateway has only about twice order-router's rps, so a retry or amplification loop is plausible.
T6.summary: Broker-gateway and order-router both departed from their in-window 09:30-09:59 baseline at the 10:00 sample, with latency and error rate rising together and both plateauing by 10:04. At one-minute resolution the two cannot be ordered, so the 'broker-gateway first' and 'order-router first' hypotheses remain open. Orchestrator latency was already around 860-950 ms before 10:00 and rises more clearly from about 10:03, so it does not show a clean step at 10:00. The 09:50 order-router deploy shows no latency or error step at 09:50. No prior-day baseline was retrieved.

Look specifically for upstream broker timeouts or 5xx, connection errors, and retry or duplicate-submission messages. Also check whether order-router logs show a change in volume or latency after the 09:50 deploy.
hints: H1 states that broker-gateway is degraded 'for a reason not yet identified'. That is a restatement of the symptom, not a root cause. No logs were queried for broker-gateway or order-router, so timeouts, 5xx responses from the upstream broker, retry storms, or errors introduced by the new order-router logging cannot be told apart.
T7.summary: broker-gateway logged slow responses from 09:46:07Z, with sustained slow GET /orders/status calls starting 10:00:03Z and rising from 331ms to about 690ms. order-router's first broker failure is an HTTP 503 at 10:00:32Z, and its timeouts (from 10:01:14Z) use thresholds that match the broker's slow durations, which points at broker-side latency as the earlier signal. broker-gateway logged no ERROR or 5xx lines in the window, so the origin of the 503s is unverified. order-router request volume did not change (rps mean 19.955), and its metric summary has no time series, so the effect of the 09:50 deploy cannot be localized.

T8.goal: Query per-queue metrics by name (depth, oldest message age, publish rate, consume rate, consumer count, unacked and redelivered counts) for outbound-msgs, inbound-msgs and portfolio-updates as time series from 09:30 to 10:30. hints: H3 was dismissed using only aggregate rabbitmq rps and error rate, which cannot show per-queue backlog. Queue depth, oldest-message age, publish versus consume rates and consumer counts for outbound-msgs, inbound-msgs and portfolio-updates were never retrieved. msg-delivery and portfolio-consumer were barely examined. T9.summary: At 1-minute resolution, broker-gateway and order-router both deviate from baseline in the same minute, 10:00 UTC, which is the reported onset. Neither shows a deviation at 09:59 or earlier, so the metrics do not show broker-gateway degrading before order-router. Broker-gateway's deviation is larger in relative terms (err_rate about 6x its 09:59 value versus about 3.8x for order-router), but the data cannot resolve sub-minute ordering. No logs were queried for this task.

T10.summary: The broker-gateway WARN+ query (09:45-10:30, not truncated, 130 lines) contains no ERROR lines, no 5xx responses, no timeouts and no connection errors. The messages are latency warnings only: 10 sporadic 'broker responded slowly once' lines, with 5 before 10:00, and about 120 'order status endpoint slow: GET /orders/status' lines from 10:00:03 onward. Those status-endpoint durations rise from 331ms to a 696ms peak around 10:04 and then hold near 620-690ms through 10:29. This points to slow broker responses on order status checks rather than broker errors, which fits the 'order pending' symptom and possibly customer retries.
